subject: tickling feet
title: What If You Tried to Tickle Yourself?

scenes.text: What if you tried to tickle yourself right now? Your brain cancels it before it starts.
Someone else's fingers on your ribs can make you scream. Your own fingers, same spot, do almost nothing.
The reason sits at the back of your brain: the cerebellum. It predicts what your own movements will feel like.
That prediction is used to dampen the touch, so brain areas for touch and feeling react much less.
Scientists tested this with a robot that tickled people on their command, with a small delay.
The longer the delay, the more it tickled. Fool your brain's timing, and you can tickle yourself.

description:
What if you tried to tickle yourself? Your cerebellum predicts the sensation of your own movements and uses that prediction to cancel the response, so it barely tickles.
In experiments where a robot passed people's own movements on with a delay, the longer the delay, the more ticklish it felt.
